items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He taught John Coltrane how to make those two notes at a time and how to make that high note on his version of Off Minor, when he had John Coltrane and Coleman Hawkins on that date with Ray Copeland and Gigi Gryce.

ctx.x: Was there a hierarchy of musicians there?

Yeah. It was Bird and Diz on the bebop scene. Miles was kind of a crown prince. He was still in his Dizzy mode. It was Monk that told Miles, you better stop playing like Dizzy and get your own stuff, because Miles was playing like Dizzy, in that he began to – so Monk told me that Miles begin to play Dizzy’s best notes. I said, wow. Then I thought of – I was doing the words to Round Midnight, and I was doing the Miles version [Hendricks sings the introduction to that version]. Then I remembered Dizzy’s version was…
Let’s go there for a moment. So Monk played other instruments as well.

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: you only have to listen to one of his solos to hear the mental agility that inspired Coltrane and everybody else.

ctx.x: Stravinsky, yeah. Because that was his favorite composer. He was an intellectual, much more than a smoker of reefer or a shoot-up jazz musician, very much more depth to him than that. And this is the part of him that I want to cover. This was a very great man. Far greater than anybody realizes. And you only have to listen to one of his solos to hear the mental agility that inspired Coltrane and everybody else. Brilliant cat.
Amazing. You’ve got some great news regarding your vocalese school?
